summary: Psalm 146 opens and closes with a summons to praise Yahweh. Between those calls, it contrasts mortal rulers, whose plans end with death, with Yahweh, who made all things, keeps truth, helps the vulnerable, and reigns forever.
whyItMatters: This psalm begins the final five-psalm cascade of praise in the Psalter. It turns praise into a question of trust: human power is temporary, but God's reign and care endure.

context.author: Anonymous within the psalm itself; Psalms is a many-author anthology formed over time.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The psalm does not identify its date of composition; the Psalter gathers poems from different periods and was shaped as a later anthology.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, near the collection's closing sequence of psalms that begin and end with praise.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew praise poetry, using direct summons, contrast, and repeated descriptions of Yahweh's actions.

outline.heading: Call to Praise
outline.note: The speaker summons the self to praise and commits to singing to God for the whole span of life.

outline.heading: Do Not Trust Mortal Power
outline.note: The psalm warns against trusting princes or any human being as ultimate help because human life and plans end.

outline.heading: Happy Hope in Yahweh
outline.note: The person whose help and hope are in Yahweh is called happy, and Yahweh is named as maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all within them.

outline.heading: Yahweh Helps the Needy
outline.note: Yahweh is described as acting for the oppressed, hungry, prisoners, blind, bowed down, righteous, foreigners, fatherless, and widow, while opposing the wicked.

outline.heading: Yahweh Reigns Forever
outline.note: The psalm ends by grounding praise in Yahweh's reign through all generations.

keyVerses.text: Don’t put your trust in princes, in a son of man in whom there is no help.
keyVerses.why: This line states the negative side of the psalm's contrast: human status and power cannot provide lasting help.

keyVerses.text: Happy is he who has the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in Yahweh, his God,
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the positive alternative: help and hope are located in Yahweh rather than in mortal rulers.

keyVerses.text: who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry. Yahweh frees the prisoners.
keyVerses.why: The verse begins the psalm's concrete list of Yahweh's care for people under pressure or need.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh will reign forever; your God, O Zion, to all generations. Praise Yah!
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers the psalm's praise into Yahweh's enduring reign.

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin by speaking to the speaker's own soul?
questions.answer: The opening line is both a call to praise and a self-address. The speaker is not only telling others what to do; the speaker is summoning the whole self into praise.

questions.question: Does the psalm say rulers are always evil?
questions.answer: No. The warning is more limited: do not put ultimate trust in princes or in any human being as the source of help. The reason given is mortality, not a claim that every ruler is wicked.

questions.question: What is the force of saying a person's thoughts perish?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says that when a human being dies, his spirit departs, he returns to the earth, and his thoughts perish that very day. In the flow of the psalm, this underlines why human power cannot bear the weight of final trust.

questions.question: Who is the God of Jacob?
questions.answer: The phrase identifies Yahweh by connection with Jacob, an ancestral figure in Israel's story. In this psalm, the phrase functions as a name for the God whose help and hope are reliable.

questions.question: Why does creation appear in a psalm about justice and help?
questions.answer: Verse 6 names Yahweh as maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them. The psalm then moves from creator language to social action, presenting Yahweh's care for the vulnerable as part of who this maker and ruler is.

questions.question: Does the psalm list literal healings, social reversals, or both?
questions.answer: The psalm says Yahweh gives food, frees prisoners, opens blind eyes, raises the bowed down, preserves foreigners, and upholds the fatherless and widow. Readers differ on whether each line should be read mainly as concrete rescue, poetic description of God's care, or both; the chapter itself presents them together as Yahweh's actions.

questions.question: Who are the foreigners, fatherless, and widow in verse 9?
questions.answer: They are named as people Yahweh preserves or upholds. The psalm does not give their individual stories; it groups them among those who lack ordinary security and are therefore singled out as recipients of God's care.

questions.question: What does it mean that Yahweh turns the way of the wicked upside down?
questions.answer: The phrase says Yahweh opposes and overturns the path of the wicked. The psalm does not describe the mechanism or timing; it simply contrasts Yahweh's support for the vulnerable with Yahweh's resistance to wickedness.

questions.question: Why does the psalm end with Zion and all generations?
questions.answer: Verse 10 addresses Zion and says Yahweh will reign forever, to all generations. The ending moves from one speaker's lifetime of praise to the continuing praise of God's people across time.

glossary.def: A short call to praise Yahweh; it frames the psalm at the beginning and end.
Human rulers or powerful people who must not become the object of ultimate trust in this psalm.
A human being; here the phrase stresses mortality and limited help.
A name for Yahweh that links the psalm's hope to Israel's ancestral story.
The community or place addressed in the final verse as Yahweh's reign is announced to all generations.
